tone_patterns: Uses formal, institutional language with an explanatory, analytical voice.
Frames sustainability as integrated into core business strategy rather than a standalone topic.
Balances risk-mitigation framing with opportunity/value-creation framing in parallel.
Employs cautious, non-absolute phrasing (e.g., indicating uncertainty, interdependence, and evolving conditions).
Uses sector-context statements to justify why the topic matters, then links back to company decision-making.
paragraph_patterns: Opens with a short contextual paragraph stating integration of sustainability across the value chain and business activities.
Introduces a conceptual model/diagram as the basis for subsequent analysis, explicitly stating its purpose as a framework.
Provides concise definitions of value-chain segments (upstream/internal operations/downstream) before deeper discussion.
Uses bullet lists to describe each segment consistently: definition, key stakeholders, relative concentration of risks/opportunities, and management implications.
Transitions from value-chain description to a broader narrative on systemic sustainability challenges and sector responsibility.
Explains characteristics of sustainability risks (interdependent, long-term, hard to quantify) before stating the assessment approach.
States the assessment lens (time horizons) and aligns it with corporate planning horizons to demonstrate governance/strategy linkage.
Ends the narrative by signaling that analysis is mapped to a limited set of material themes, acting as a bridge to subsequent tables.
heading_patterns: Uses hierarchical numbering for subsections (e.g., section.subsection) to support navigation.
Headings are descriptive and topic-led (value chain risks & opportunities; time horizons; material theme mapping).
Includes a standalone subheading introducing time horizons, followed by a short lead-in sentence and then bullets.
Figure captions follow a consistent label format (e.g., 'Figure X: ...') placed adjacent to the visual.
table_patterns: Uses a two-part table structure: (1) impact materiality split into positive vs negative impacts with an 'actual/potential' qualifier; (2) financial materiality split into risks vs opportunities with associated timeframes.
Table headers are multi-level: a top header indicating the materiality lens, then subheaders for categories (positive/negative; risks/opportunities).
Rows use short, titled impact/risk/opportunity statements followed by brief explanatory text.
Includes a separate column or field to classify each item by status (actual vs potential) and/or timeframe (short/medium/long).
Timeframe entries are expressed as ranges (e.g., short-to-medium) rather than single points, reinforcing uncertainty and planning horizons.
Tables are introduced after narrative setup and appear to anchor the section’s analytical claims.
figure_or_diagram_patterns: Includes a conceptual value-chain diagram that visually segments upstream, internal operations, and downstream.
Diagram combines process flow labels with stakeholder nodes (e.g., investors/suppliers/employees/clients) to show where risks/opportunities arise.
Uses short callout text blocks near the diagram to define each segment and its risk meaning.
Figure is referenced in the narrative as the foundational framework for analysis.
pdf_layout_patterns: Section spans multiple pages with consistent footer elements: section label, page number, and report title line.
Figure occupies a prominent portion of the page, with caption and explanatory callouts positioned close to the visual.
Bulleted lists are used to break dense content and improve scanability, often with hanging indents and short lead phrases.
Subheading and bullet list for time horizons appears as a distinct block, visually separated from preceding narrative.
Tables appear on a dedicated page or as a dominant element, with clear column separation and bold headers.
Consistent typographic hierarchy: numbered headings, subheadings, body text, bullets, and labeled figure/table elements.
disclosure_language_patterns: Uses definitional language to clarify scope (e.g., what upstream/internal/downstream mean in the value chain).
Explicitly states methodological framing (conceptual model as a base framework; time horizons used for analysis).
Connects sustainability considerations to strategic planning and decision-making processes.
Uses classification language aligned to materiality concepts (impact vs financial; actual vs potential; risk vs opportunity).
Avoids definitive predictions; emphasizes uncertainty, evolving regulation/markets, and long-term nature of sustainability topics.
evidence_presentation_patterns: Presents a logical chain: conceptual model → segment definitions → qualitative assessment of concentration/criticality → time-horizon lens → tabulated impacts/risks/opportunities.
Uses comparative qualifiers (e.g., relative concentration, most/least critical segment) without relying on quantitative proof in the narrative.
Supports narrative claims with structured artifacts (figure and tables) rather than citations.
Uses categorization (actual/potential; timeframe bands) as the primary evidence scaffolding.
section_specific_observations: The section functions as a bridge between high-level strategy integration statements and detailed materiality/risk-opportunity disclosures.
Value-chain framing is used to organize sustainability topics by where they arise and how they propagate through the business model.
Time horizons are treated as an explicit analytical tool and are disclosed in a standardized, repeatable format.
Materiality is operationalized through tabular classification rather than extended narrative.
things_to_avoid_copying: Any company name, report title line, or branded figure/table labels tied to the reference entity.
Any sector-specific claims presented as unique positioning or competitive advantage.
Any exact time-horizon year ranges or labels as written; use the pattern but define ranges appropriate to the new report.
Any specific material themes count or naming, and any specific risk/opportunity examples tied to the reference context.
Any statements implying quantified outcomes or performance without supporting data in the new report.
content_specific_items_detected_and_excl: Specific business lines and product/service categories listed in the value-chain diagram.
Specific time-horizon year cutoffs and labels.
Specific material theme naming and count.
Specific example risks/opportunities/impacts (e.g., regulatory cost, greenwashing, market exclusion, investor attraction) and their stated timeframes.
